questions.stem: A client is waiting in a cold exam room. Which change in the blood vessels of the skin should the nurse expect?
options: They widen, to bring warm blood to the skin
They narrow, to keep warm blood in the body's core
They don't change, since the heart is what responds to cold
They widen, to cool the core
questions.rationale:
In the cold, sympathetic signals narrow the skin's vessels, keeping warm blood in the core (which is why cold fingers can look pale).

Widening the skin's vessels lets heat escape, the response to warmth. The vessels do respond to cold, through the sympathetic nerves.

Takeaway: Cold: skin vessels narrow; heat: they widen.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing what sets the blood pressure. Which change should the nurse expect to raise it?
options: A slower heart rate
Widening of the arterioles
A smaller blood volume after bleeding
Narrowing of the arterioles
questions.rationale:
Blood pressure rises with the heart's output (rate and force) and with resistance. Narrower arterioles resist the flow more, so the pressure rises.

A slower heart rate and a smaller blood volume lower the output, and widening the arterioles lowers the resistance: all three lower the blood pressure.

Takeaway: Blood pressure = output × resistance.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing blood pressure regulation. For each change, click to specify its effect on the blood pressure.
rows: The blood volume drops after bleeding
questions.rationale:
A faster rate and narrower arterioles raise the pressure. Weaker contractions, a smaller blood volume, and wider arterioles lower it.

Thinking a smaller volume raises the pressure is a mistake: less blood in the vessels means less pressure.

Takeaway: Rate, force, volume, and narrowing push the pressure up; their opposites bring it down.

questions.stem: A client is jogging. Which changes should the nurse expect?
options: Narrower blood vessels to the digestive tract
Narrower airways, to slow the breathing
Stronger heart contractions
Wider blood vessels in the leg muscles
A slower heart rate, from vagus nerve signals
A faster heart rate
questions.rationale:
Exercise brings a sympathetic response: a faster, stronger heart, wider vessels in the working muscles, and narrower vessels to the gut, sending blood where it's needed.

A slower heart rate is the parasympathetic effect, at rest. The airways widen, rather than narrow, during exercise.

Takeaway: Exercise: more blood, pumped harder, sent to the muscles.

questions.stem: During deep sleep, a healthy client's heart rate drops to 52/min. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Vagus nerve (parasympathetic) signals slow the heart at rest.”
“Sympathetic signals slow the heart to save energy at night.”
“The heart's muscle weakens during sleep and can't beat faster.”
“The blood volume falls at night, so the heart beats less often.”
questions.rationale:
At rest, parasympathetic signals through the vagus nerve slow the heart, and a healthy heart rate can fall into the 50s during sleep.

Sympathetic signals speed the heart, rather than slow it. The muscle doesn't weaken, and the blood volume doesn't fall overnight.

Takeaway: Rest and digest: parasympathetic, slower heart.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the sympathetic nervous system. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: When the sympathetic nervous system is activated, the heart rate {{0}}, the heart contracts {{1}}, and the blood vessels in the skin {{2}}.

options: falls
rises
doesn't change
less forcefully
irregularly
more forcefully
narrow
widen
stay the same

questions.rationale:
Sympathetic activation raises the heart rate, makes the heart contract more forcefully, and narrows the skin's vessels, raising the blood pressure.

Choosing widen is a mistake for the skin: the vessels to the working muscles widen, but those in the skin and gut narrow.

Takeaway: Sympathetic: faster, stronger, skin vessels narrow.

questions.stem: A client asks why a high HDL cholesterol is good for the heart. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “HDL carries cholesterol away from the arteries, back to the liver.”
“HDL widens the arteries so that blood flows through them more easily.”
“HDL thins the blood so clots form less often.”
“HDL turns into LDL cholesterol, which the body needs for energy.”
questions.rationale:
HDL (“good” cholesterol) carries cholesterol away from the artery walls back to the liver, which protects against plaque. An HDL under 40 (men) or 50 (women) is a risk factor.

HDL doesn't widen arteries or thin the blood, and it doesn't turn into LDL, which carries cholesterol to the arteries.

Takeaway: HDL: high is protective. LDL: high is a risk.

questions.stem: A client says, “I switched to coconut oil for all my cooking because it's natural.” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “That's a good choice, since natural oils are heart-healthy for most people.”
“It's a tropical oil, high in saturated fat; olive or avocado oil is better.”
“That's fine, as long as you also use butter on most days of the week.”
“Coconut oil is best for frying, since it doesn't break down at high heat.”
questions.rationale:
Coconut and palm oil are tropical oils, high in saturated fat. The heart-healthy choices are unsaturated: extra-virgin olive oil, avocado oil, and other non-tropical vegetable oils.

Being natural doesn't make an oil heart-healthy. Butter is another saturated fat, and choosing an oil for frying misses the point of heart-healthy eating.

Takeaway: Heart-healthy oils: olive, avocado, non-tropical vegetable. Not coconut or palm.

questions.stem: A client with high blood pressure asks why limiting sodium helps. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Sodium makes your heart beat faster and harder, raising the pressure.”
“Sodium narrows your arteries the moment you eat it.”
“Sodium holds extra water in your blood, raising the pressure.”
“Sodium thickens your blood, so it clots more easily.”
questions.rationale:
Water follows sodium: extra sodium holds more water in the blood vessels, so the blood volume and pressure rise.

Sodium doesn't directly speed the heart, narrow the arteries right away, or make the blood clot.

Takeaway: Less sodium, less water held, lower pressure.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' histories. Which client should the nurse identify as having the most risk factors for cardiovascular disease?
options: A 38-year-old who doesn't smoke, with a BMI of 23 and an LDL of 96
A 45-year-old runner with an HDL of 62 and a blood pressure of 118/74 mm Hg
A 52-year-old with a BMI of 27 and a total cholesterol of 188
A 62-year-old with diabetes who smokes and has a blood pressure of 148/92
questions.rationale:
The 62-year-old has four of the instructor's risk factors: age, diabetes, smoking, and high blood pressure.

The 52-year-old has one (a BMI over 25; a total cholesterol under 200 isn't a risk factor). The runner's HDL of 62 is protective, and the 38-year-old's findings are all within healthy limits.

Takeaway: CVD risk: high blood pressure, cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, low HDL, smoking, diabetes, age, BMI over 25.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's results. For each finding, click to specify whether it's a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.
rows: Smokes half a pack a day
questions.rationale:
An LDL over 100, a BMI over 25, and smoking are risk factors. An HDL of 62 is protective, and a total cholesterol under 200 and a blood pressure of 116/74 are within healthy limits.

Calling a high HDL a risk is a mistake: it's the low HDL (under 40 for men, 50 for women) that raises the risk.

Takeaway: LDL over 100: risk. HDL low: risk; HDL high: protective.

questions.stem: A client asks for a heart-healthy breakfast. Which choice should the nurse suggest?
options: Oatmeal with fruit and low-fat milk
White toast with butter and jam
A croissant with a glass of whole milk
Eggs and bacon fried in palm oil
questions.rationale:
Oatmeal is a whole grain, and low-fat milk is the heart-healthy dairy choice.

White toast is a refined grain with saturated fat from the butter. A croissant and whole milk are high in saturated fat, and palm oil is a tropical oil.

Takeaway: Whole grains, low-fat dairy, unsaturated oils, low sodium.

questions.stem: A client asks why diabetes raises the risk of heart disease. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “High glucose damages the vessel walls, speeding up plaque buildup.”
“Insulin raises your cholesterol each time you eat a meal.”
“Diabetes slows your heart rate, so less blood reaches the heart muscle.”
“High glucose thins your blood, so your heart works harder.”
questions.rationale:
Over time, a high glucose damages the lining of the blood vessels, which speeds up atherosclerosis (plaque) in the heart's arteries and elsewhere.

Insulin doesn't raise cholesterol with each meal, diabetes doesn't slow the heart rate, and glucose doesn't thin the blood.

Takeaway: Diabetes harms the vessels: a major CVD risk factor.

questions.stem: A client's right ventricle is failing. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Crackles in both lungs
Bulging neck veins
An enlarged, tender liver
Shortness of breath when lying flat
Swelling of both ankles
questions.rationale:
When the right ventricle fails, blood backs up into the body's veins: swollen ankles, bulging neck veins, and an enlarged liver.

Crackles and shortness of breath lying flat come from fluid in the lungs, when the left ventricle fails.

Takeaway: Right-sided failure: the body swells. Left-sided: the lungs fill.

questions.stem: A client with a deep vein thrombosis asks what an embolus is. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “A weak spot in an artery wall that balloons out.”
“A narrowing of an artery caused by plaque.”
“A clot that stays attached to the wall of the vein where it formed.”
“A clot, or other mass, that breaks loose and travels in the blood.”
questions.rationale:
A thrombus is a clot attached where it formed. An embolus is a clot (or other mass) that breaks loose and travels, like a leg clot that lodges in the lungs.

A clot that stays attached is the thrombus. A ballooning artery is an aneurysm, and a plaque narrowing is atherosclerosis.

Takeaway: Thrombus stays; embolus travels.

questions.stem: A client asks what an aneurysm is. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “A clot that blocks one of the arteries to the brain.”
“A blood vessel that has gone into spasm.”
“A weak area of an artery wall that balloons out.”
“A valve that lets blood leak backward.”
questions.rationale:
An aneurysm is a weakened area of an artery wall that balloons out, which can rupture, often linked to high blood pressure, smoking, and atherosclerosis.

A clot blocking an artery is a thrombus or embolus, a spasm is a sudden tightening, and a leaking valve causes a murmur.

Takeaway: Aneurysm: a bulging weak spot that can burst.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing cerebrovascular accidents. For each description, click to specify the problem the nurse should recognize.
rows: A clot blocks an artery in the brain
A weak artery in the brain bursts
One-sided weakness clears within an hour, with no lasting damage
A clot from the heart travels to the brain
questions.rationale:
An ischemic stroke is a blocked artery (by a clot formed there or one that traveled). A hemorrhagic stroke is a burst artery. A TIA is a brief blockage whose symptoms clear without lasting damage, a warning sign.

Calling a traveling clot hemorrhagic is a mistake: it blocks the artery, so the stroke is ischemic.

Takeaway: Blocked: ischemic. Burst: hemorrhagic. Brief and gone: TIA, a warning.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a murmur over a client's heart. Which of the following could cause it?
options: Slow, smooth flow through healthy valves
Very fast blood flow, as in a high fever
A blocked coronary artery
A valve that doesn't close fully
A narrowed (stenotic) valve
questions.rationale:
A murmur is the sound of turbulent blood flow: through a narrowed valve, backward through a valve that doesn't close, or when the flow is very fast, as in a fever or anemia.

Smooth flow through healthy valves is silent. A blocked coronary artery starves the heart muscle (a heart attack); it doesn't by itself make a murmur.

Takeaway: Murmur = turbulence: narrow valves, leaky valves, or fast flow.

questions.stem: A clot blocks an artery on the left side of a client's brain. Which finding should the nurse expect?
options: Weakness of both legs but not the arms
Loss of vision in both eyes
Weakness of the left arm and leg
Weakness of the right arm and leg
questions.rationale:
Each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body, so a left-sided stroke weakens the right arm and leg (and often affects speech).

Left-sided weakness comes from a right-sided stroke. Weakness of both legs points to the spinal cord, and a single clot rarely takes vision in both eyes.

Takeaway: The brain controls the opposite side of the body.

questions.stem: A client with severe heart failure is making less urine. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Less blood flows to the kidneys, so they make less urine
The kidneys are holding glucose, which blocks the urine
The bladder can't contract well because the heart muscle is weak
The extra fluid is leaving through the lungs instead
questions.rationale:
When the heart pumps poorly, less blood reaches the kidneys, so they make less urine and hold on to salt and water, one of the body-wide impacts of cardiovascular dysfunction.

Glucose doesn't block urine, the bladder's emptying doesn't depend on the heart's strength, and fluid isn't lost through the lungs in place of urine.

Takeaway: A weak pump means less blood to every organ, the kidneys included.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client for a deep vein thrombosis in the calf. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible signs?
options: Warmth over the calf
Calf pain or tenderness
Redness over the area
Swelling of one calf
A cool, pale foot with a weak pulse
Swelling of both ankles
questions.rationale:
A DVT blocks the blood's return from the leg, so the calf is swollen, warm, painful, and red, usually on one side.

A cool, pale foot with a weak pulse points to too little arterial flow. Swelling of both ankles suggests a body-wide cause, like heart failure.

Takeaway: DVT: one leg, swollen, warm, red, painful.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing risk factors. Which one most raises the risk of a hemorrhagic stroke?
options: A high HDL cholesterol level
Uncontrolled high blood pressure
A slow resting heart rate of 54/min
A low blood glucose
questions.rationale:
Years of uncontrolled high blood pressure weaken the small arteries of the brain until one bursts: the main risk factor for a hemorrhagic stroke.

A high HDL is protective, a slow resting heart rate is common in fit people, and a low glucose causes confusion but not a bleed.

Takeaway: High blood pressure: the leading risk for a brain bleed.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks what a capillary refill test measures. Which answer should the nurse give?
options: How much oxygen the blood is carrying to the tissues
How well blood reaches the fingertips and toes
How fast and how regularly the heart is beating
How thick the blood is and how easily it clots
questions.rationale:
Capillary refill shows how quickly color returns after the nail bed is pressed: a measure of blood flow to the small vessels (peripheral perfusion). Under 3 seconds is expected.

Oxygen is measured by pulse oximetry, the heart rate by the pulse, and the blood's thickness by lab tests.

Takeaway: Capillary refill: peripheral perfusion; under 3 seconds.

questions.stem: A client's capillary refill is 4 seconds in the toes of the left foot and 2 seconds in the right. Which interpretation should the nurse make?
options: Both feet are within the expected range
The right foot has reduced blood flow
The left foot has reduced blood flow, which needs follow-up
The client is dehydrated, which slows the refill in both feet
questions.rationale:
A refill over 3 seconds is slow, and the difference between feet points to reduced blood flow to the left foot, which needs follow-up (pulses, color, temperature).

4 seconds is outside the expected range. The right foot's 2 seconds is expected, and dehydration would slow both feet, not one.

Takeaway: Compare sides: a slow refill on one side points to that limb.

questions.stem: A nurse checks a client's capillary refill in a cold room. Which effect should the nurse expect the cold to have?
options: It can make the refill look slower than it is
It can make the refill look faster than it is
It has no effect on the refill time
It makes the nail bed easier to blanch
questions.rationale:
Cold narrows the small vessels of the fingers and toes, so the refill can look slower than it is. Warm the hand or foot and recheck.

Cold doesn't speed the refill, and it does affect it, through the narrowed vessels. It doesn't change how easily the nail blanches.

Takeaway: Cold fingers can give a falsely slow refill.

questions.stem: A client's calf aches while walking and eases within a few minutes of rest. Which problem should the nurse suspect?
options: Venous insufficiency
A deep vein thrombosis
A muscle strain from exercise
Arterial insufficiency
questions.rationale:
Pain while walking that eases with rest (intermittent claudication) means the working muscles need more blood than narrowed arteries can deliver: arterial insufficiency.

Venous insufficiency causes aching and swelling that eases when the legs are raised. A DVT hurts at rest too, and a strain doesn't ease predictably within minutes.

Takeaway: Pain with walking, relief with rest: arterial.

questions.stem: A client has a painful sore on the tip of a toe, with a pale, dry base and little drainage. Which problem does this sore suggest?
options: A pressure injury from bed rest
A burn from a heating pad
Venous insufficiency
Arterial insufficiency
questions.rationale:
A painful sore at the tip of a toe, with a pale, dry base, fits arterial insufficiency: too little blood reaches the tissue.

Venous sores are usually near the inner ankle, moist, and less painful. Nothing here points to a pressure injury or a burn.

Takeaway: Arterial sores: toes, pale, dry, painful. Venous: inner ankle, moist.
